headline: Russia/Tinkov investment: right on the company fundamentals, wrong on country tail risk — Russia discount was warranted; lesson is to stress-test extreme scenarios including 5% probability events that can permanently impair capital
reasoning: Iona held Tinkov, a high-quality Russian digital bank serving underbanked consumers, which was performing extremely well operationally and was attractively valued given the Russia discount. When Russia invaded Ukraine all of that became irrelevant and the position was a total loss. The lesson was that being right on the company is insufficient if you are not humble enough about country-level tail risk and black swan scenarios. She now insists on stress-testing both bull and bear cases from first principles, including low-probability events that could permanently impair 100% of capital.
quote: So in Russia, it was an emerging market bank basically and it was an extraordinary business. Frankly, one of the best digital banks I had seen and amazing customer proposition, amazing, NPS scores to kind of just solving. It was a digital bank in Russia. So it started off actually as kind of credit cards and debit cards for the lower and less affluent population... When Russia invaded Ukraine, I learned you can be completely right about the company but still have a disastrous investment because you were insufficiently humble about the country and the tail risk as well. So the lesson for me was just to be very creative in both the bull and the bear case and really stress test the numbers and not just put through a bear case in these scenarios that we've seen historically... you have to put in a bull case. If you had just put in a bull case from the past 10 years, you would have completely missed this trade. So I think you've got to think outside the box from first principles about what the real risks are and even the 5% probability outcome that could permanently impair 100% of your capital.

So it's something to be considered very, very carefully if you're looking down that option. And in my view, it's not really workable because of risks like that.

headline: The 52-week high is an irrational anchor: professional investors buy what retail investors sell near that level

Despite this, it exerts strong psychological power through anchoring and reference dependence, causing everyday investors to feel uncomfortable and want to sell when a stock approaches that level. He notes that professionals tend to be on the other side of those trades, happily buying what retail sells. He frames this as a classic rational-actor versus human-behaviour split, driven by heuristics and gut feelings rather than rigorous analysis.
quote: The 52 week high is just a number. So why does it hold power over us? It's a great question, right? Because rationally it shouldn't. It means absolutely nothing. But I think it's a fascinating thing about how we as humans interact... the rational actor does things mathematically and does them rationally and considered and researched and rigorous. And then the humans do things with heuristics, rules of thumb. We get gut feelings. And I think the 52 week high ends up playing on a few of those, but in particular, the concept of anchoring.

headline: Individual investors consistently mistimed — buying after runs and replacing sold stocks with ones that go up even more; doing the opposite of the crowd may offer an edge
reasoning: Andrew Grant notes that individual investors lack the full information set and analytical capability of professional investors, leaving them working with limited data. Behavioural finance research shows retail investors are poor at timing: they tend to buy stocks that have already risen too much, and when they sell, they replace those positions with stocks that subsequently appreciate even further. This implies a contrarian signal — buying what individuals want to sell and selling what they want to buy may generate excess returns. The utility derived from selling at a profit also reinforces the disposition effect, making investors reluctant to sell at a loss even when it would be rational.
quote: Research in behavioral finance shows that individuals aren't good at timing their decisions. Right. So in other words, they'll buy stocks after they've gone up too much. headline: USD structural debasement thesis: financial repression and sustained negative real yields are the only politically viable exit from a fiscal debt trap, making the dollar the pressure valve
reasoning: The US has a spending problem compounded by politically entrenched entitlements (social security, federal health, veterans' benefits) and interest payments that already consume 98.4% of annual tax receipts and are growing at a 5.7% CAGR — far exceeding the CBO's 3.9% nominal GDP growth forecast. Austerity is politically impermissible and defaulting on debt would destroy bond markets. The only viable path is financial repression: pinning nominal rates below inflation to erode the real debt burden, as the US did from 1945–1980. Under the current floating dollar regime, the currency must absorb this adjustment. Historical data from the IMF and Reinhart & Rogoff shows roughly 80% of net-debtor countries with debt/GDP above 120% suffered a sovereign default, inflation crisis, or currency crash within a decade. The fund is explicitly building a margin of safety in its global portfolio against USD exposure given this macro setup.
quote: The United States undoubtedly has a spending problem. Ultimately, this problem is compounded by a pernicious permission structure across the American political divide which optimises for short-term sugar hits like unfunded tax cuts, expanded entitlements and one-off transfers as band-aid workarounds to paper over the long-term cracks of the country's significantly deteriorating fiscal outlook... We believe any attempt at true austerity would significantly hurt U.S. equity markets whilst defaulting on debt would have a similar effect on the U.S. bond market. Given the mass citizen wealth tied up in U.S. equities and the widespread perception of U.S. paper as risk-free, we believe both options are, at their core, politically impermissible. This perfect storm affords the U.S. only one real avenue to veer from its disastrous fiscal trajectory. That is financial repression and sustained negative real yields by pinning nominal rates below inflation. Given today's floating U.S. dollar regime, the currency must be the valve to print their way out of this impending crisis.

headline: Structurally bearish on the US dollar: applying a 10% per annum currency discount to all US-dollar-denominated earnings to reflect risk of fiscal repression leaking into a weaker exchange rate
reasoning: The fund argues that with US Debt-to-GDP above 120%, PPI inflation at 5.4%, the 10-year yield near 5%, and potential $1.2T in new stimulus (Trump's $5,000 adult dividend proposal), the US fiscal outlook is deteriorating rapidly. The firm expects a large share of foreign and domestic asset holders to diversify away from US dollars as this dynamic becomes clearer. To manage this risk without direct currency hedging, they apply a 10% per annum translation haircut to future earnings and free cash flow predominantly denominated in USD, and only invest after this adjustment if a stock still offers 75–100% upside over 2–3 years.

We apply a 10% per annum currency discount to our view of a business's future earnings power and free cash flow generation whereby the bulk of these earnings are denominated within the United States. To be clear, this haircut is not a view that these businesses will earn 10% less in U.S. dollar terms. Instead, it is a translation adjustment whereby we mark down the base-currency value of these U.S. dollar earnings by 10% per annum to reflect the risk that repression under a floating dollar regime will leak into a structurally weaker exchange rate. headline: Global economy shifting from an age of efficiency to 'plasticity' — rewiring supply chains, trade, finance and production away from just-in-time specialisation toward resilience, with AI-driven productivity acceleration as the base case
reasoning: Waller argues the global economy is navigating multiple choke points — most recently the closure of the Strait of Hormuz — that are forcing a structural shift from the decades-long model of specialisation and globalisation toward a focus on resilience. He draws an analogy with neuroplasticity: just as the brain rewires itself after disruption, the global economy is rerouting around financial and physical bottlenecks. This 'great rewiring' is expected to play out across trade, finance and production over the next five years. The base case also includes an acceleration of AI diffusion that is expected to drive productivity gains and broader prosperity.
quote: So in a nutshell, we believe that we are moving from an age of efficiency to an age of what we call plasticity. So back in the day at university, next to economics, I also completed a course in cognitive neuroscience. And there I really learned that the brain is able to rewire itself after a disruption. And likewise, the global economy today, which is clearly faced by a lot of choke points, is also working its way around those financial and physical choke points. At the latest physical choke point, of course, being the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. So we are moving from an economy that has been fully being focused on specialization, benefiting from decades of globalization, from an abundance of labor, to a world that is now focusing on resilience instead of being just in time and being over-specialized. And that's basically the great rewiring, which takes place on multiple fronts in trade, in finance and in production.

headline: AI-driven workforce disruption is creating acute financial vulnerability for executive women, requiring 6–12 month emergency cash buffers and proactive debt elimination
reasoning: Katrina Pulbrook notes that six executive women clients reached out in two weeks after redundancy, with roles in project work, administration and technical fields particularly exposed to AI displacement. She argues that high earners often take on proportionally large financial commitments (mortgages, personal loans, car leases, family obligations), meaning income loss is especially devastating. Her five-step preparedness framework centres on: building 6–12 months of emergency cash, auditing discretionary spending, eliminating non-deductible debt, seeking professional financial and accounting advice, and continuous upskilling. She emphasises that redundancy is not a personal failure but a structural workforce shift that will continue, and that having financial breathing room is critical to avoiding panic-driven decisions.
quote: The preparation is really in five steps. And the first one is, um, you know, basically what we want to do is make sure we've got an emergency cash buffer that's really, really important. So that's usually 6 to 12 months worth of your income that's sitting there that you can lean on for the future. The second one is making sure that you understand what all your commitments are, and these are not the regular ones such as mortgage, etc. these are more around the other expenses that we do on a day to day basis, where we might be a little bit more frivolous than most. The third one is making sure that we eliminate any unnecessary non deductible debt. And this is not just the mortgages because we've got to live somewhere. But there's also things personal loans, credit cards you know high leases on cars. Have a look at those and think in the dream of me not having a job, how would I cope with paying for all of these as well?

Crucially, this upward pressure on real rates is independent of how the CapEx is financed — debt, retained earnings or equity all consume the same real resources. The financing channel matters for asset prices and risk allocation but not for the macroeconomic arithmetic linking saving, investment and equilibrium real rates.

Unless desired saving rises commensurately, equilibrium real rates must increase until desired saving rises. Some investment is crowded out or both.

reasoning: Hugh Gimbah outlines that bond markets are now pricing three additional hikes from the Fed, ECB, and Bank of Japan, and nearly four from the Bank of England, over the next 12 months. He frames this as a tweaking cycle rather than a major tightening regime, arguing that if oil stays around $100 and growth holds, central banks will continue hiking at a roughly quarterly pace until inflation meaningfully declines. If oil prices fall back toward $80, the hiking narrative could reverse quickly, with 2% inflation back in sight for 2027. The risk of slipping into a sustained hiking cycle increases if economic resilience begins to show up in labour market strength.
quote: If we're going to hover with oil prices and let's say a hundred dollars a barrel where you have inflation pressure clearly coming through from higher energy prices but you also have growth holding up pretty well sort of where we are today that's probably the easiest path that allows the central banks to be able to continue to hike and I think important to say here that three or four hikes in the context of history is not a major hiking cycle that would fall into the sort of tweaks around the edges category rather than something where they're seriously trying to slow down the economy substantially to get inflation down... I do personally think it's feasible that you could see the central banks slipping into this roughly quarterly pace of rate hikes until you get more significant progress in the Middle East.

headline: Deep-rooted political discontent across Western electorates unlikely to improve; centrist politics is harder to sustain, but fractious coalitions tend to produce minor rather than major policy change, limiting actual economic impact
reasoning: Karen Ward argues that political discontent in Western electorates is structural and unlikely to resolve soon, with polarisation driving voters toward more extreme parties. However, she notes that unstable coalitions and fractious politics tend to constrain rather than enable major policy shifts, meaning headline political risk often overstates economic risk. The bond market, she argues, acts as judge, jury and executioner in disciplining politicians toward better fiscal behaviour, but this also implies higher volatility in bond markets and higher interest rates as a result. Investors should discount political headlines but remain alert to the bond market's role in course-correcting fiscal excesses.
quote: I think it's clear that it's really hard to be a centrist politician these days. You know the centrist offering just doesn't have the appeal when you've got this deep-rooted discontent and these more extreme parties willing to offer an alternative way. So that probably means we are in this world of you know coalitions being difficult to not only form but maintain... But it also reminds us that when we hear particularly from very extreme politicians their ability to actually follow through on their agenda is pretty limited. So I think it's just another demonstration of how the politics on the headline level looks pretty worrisome but when you start to break it down into what it means for the economy it perhaps is less so.

headline: Oil at $100/barrel despite escalating Middle East conflict because ~17 million barrels per day still flowing via alternative routes — ship-to-ship transfers, UAE/Oman southern ports, and Saudi west coast — out of a pre-conflict 23 million bpd baseline
reasoning: Hugh Gimbah explains the divergence between alarming geopolitical headlines and a relatively contained oil price by pointing to the volume of crude still moving out of the Middle East through alternative channels. Prior to the conflict, around 23 million barrels per day left the region, predominantly through the Strait of Hormuz. Despite the conflict, approximately 17 million barrels per day can still be accounted for through ship-to-ship transfers, southern UAE and Oman ports, and (until recently) increased flows from Saudi Arabia's west coast. While $100/barrel is not ideal, it is far below what one might expect given the severity of the headlines, and all major parties — including the US, Iran, and China — retain an economic interest in preventing a global recession.
quote: When we now add up all of the different ways the oil is still leaving the Middle East we can explain about 17 million barrels per day of that 23 still getting out. And so the composition has changed because you've had a much greater dependency on some of these alternative ports so again whether that's the south coast of the UAE or the south coast of Oman we're seeing a big pickup in what's known as ship-to-ship transit so this is where local ships are just doing the straights for moves leg and then parking up an alternative port to then connect into those global supply chains... all in all I think this is still the right way to think through this conflict where obviously the politics of the situation is still extremely difficult the headlines are still challenging and let's be clear $100 a barrel oil is not great news for the economy when it's coming through these supply concerns but ultimately I think it's just understanding that there's a lot more oil that's been moving than you would expect if you've just been reading the headlines in the FT.

quote: I think for markets where it becomes really important is the absolutely pivotal role of the bond market because when the political setup is an ideal the bond market acts as judge jury and sometimes arceles-tross executioner the bond market will be that adjudicate on the political system to say no I don't like what you're doing here... certainly much more volatility in the bond market and higher interest rates as a result of it. And I guess the challenge here is that we know bond yields are rising everywhere big moves all parts of the curve so far in 2026 but trying to break down the extent to which bond yields are rising because of some of these political challenges versus actually pretty strong growth versus actually quite high levels of inflation is really hard.

headline: AI represents genuine exponential change warranting a dedicated portfolio sleeve, even at high valuations, because the 10-year transformation potential justifies paying prices that would be indefensible in a normal environment
reasoning: Perold argues that AI-driven change is genuinely exponential and that high prices are actually consistent with things going very well. He recommends creating a dedicated AI sleeve to free oneself from constant cross-comparison with non-AI investments. He acknowledges the danger of 'this time is different' reasoning but believes it is warranted here. Even if only a quarter or half of the AI potential materialises, the outcome would still be profound. The key discipline is thinking long term and being comfortable holding high-priced assets in a way that would be irrational in a conventional environment.
quote: You're seeing companies with extraordinary earnings growth, high valuations. We're seeing venture investments in the many billions. 20 billion value, 5 billion before. How do you decide those? How do you think about investing in a world where the underlying fundamentals are changing very quickly but the price is very high? If the price was low, would you believe it was changing? Because the price is high, it's consistent with things going really well. When the price is high, you always recoil. Part of you needs to say something like, AI is going to work. Ten years from now, we'll be in a world we won't recognize. It may not be the case. That's possible. Maybe only half of that's possible. It's still profound. Maybe only a quarter is possible. It's still profound. If I think that's true, it means that I need to think long term and be comfortable owning things at high prices, knowing that in any normal investment environment, you'd never own them because this is different. Those are the most dangerous words in investing, saying this time is different. But this time is different.

headline: Large-cap PE faces a structural triple squeeze: high entry multiples, insufficient carry to retain talent, and fundraising headwinds for Fund N+1 — talent and deal flow migrating down the market cap spectrum
reasoning: Perold explains that the carry problem is most acute at the large end of PE where entry multiples were highest and realisation timelines have extended. Many large-cap managers will struggle to generate hurdle-clearing returns, causing talent to leave for better opportunities. This is feeding the wave of independent and fundless sponsors at the lower middle market level. He is not bullish on allocating to large-cap PE as a result.
quote: PE is not a breeding ground for public firms. It's a place for concentrated ownership to own, fix up, and create a firm from A to B. Then you exit either to a strategic or to another PE firm, sell them, you go public. Increasingly, it's the same owner wants to hang on to it. That leads to continuation vehicles, GP led, secondaries, same thing. Because it's private for longer, then fewer realizations, so there's much less carry. You've had a phenomenon that people tended to overpay a few years ago. Those are going to struggle to hurdle and generate carry. If you're working at one of these firms, what do you do? Is it worth hanging on for a small carry or you go somewhere else for a better opportunity?

There are deposits people put up and you get the deposits the minute you cross thresholds. The collateral is directly or indirectly related to a hyperscaler often. headline: GP-led continuation vehicles are a rich hunting ground for gem businesses at attractive prices, driven by structural DPI pressure forcing sponsors to recycle capital without selling their best assets
reasoning: Perold explains that low DPI is preventing many PE sponsors from raising Fund N+1, pushing them toward continuation vehicles as a way to return cash to existing LPs while retaining their best assets. High Vista has built a dedicated team to underwrite these directly. The lower middle market CVs are especially attractive because entry prices are lower and multiple expansion potential is greater. By definition the assets being put into CVs are the ones sponsors most want to keep, creating a bias toward quality.
quote: In the continuation vehicles, we've hired a team that is now directly looking at continuation vehicles. The beauty there is you can find these gem businesses. If you're a PE sponsor and you have a gem business, there's much more to be done with the business. You can keep rolling up stuff. You can keep adding to it and get a much higher value down the road. Why do you want to sell it? Someone has to take that business and continue to morph it. You're in the best position to do that. Better you keep it and fix it. Yet you want DPI. The continuation vehicle is a way to bring in new investors to take out investors who want out.

headline: Short-duration software loans are likely fine despite equity multiple compression driven by terminal value uncertainty — credit investors need EBITDA only through loan maturity, not beyond
reasoning: Perold uses Salesforce as an illustration of how AI disruption is compressing terminal value multiples even for high-growth software companies. However, he argues that credit investors in software are largely insulated because loans are short-dated and only require the company to generate enough cash to repay principal — not to sustain a high terminal value. He believes concern about software private credit is overblown for this reason.

We think a lot of the software will be okay because the credit's the short-term loans. They're not long dated. The software you just needed to pay off within a few years and you're going to be okay. It's not like if you own a software firm where if you own the equity, the terminal value of that software firm is critical. Terminal value at a time of disruption is one of the hardest things to sort out.

headline: Micro- and small-cap biotech is a 'beautifully inefficient' market where small specialists can generate outsized returns precisely because large capital is structurally constrained from trading actively
reasoning: Perold identifies micro-cap and small-cap biotech as a structural alpha opportunity because the companies are binary — they either fail and die or succeed and get acquired by large pharma. Large funds are forced into buy-and-hold due to liquidity constraints, while small specialist managers can trade around events and earn excess returns. High Vista backs small, early-stage specialist managers in this space, often spinning out from larger firms, and exits when asset growth compromises their ability to be nimble.
quote: Biotech equities, micro-cap, small-cap biotech stocks. They're all burning money in pursuit of a therapy, or two, or three. They're either going to die if it fails, or if they succeed, they'll get sold to pharma. They'll sell them having revenues. They're burning money, they're diluting shareholders, capital inefficient, risky, and you need to know the signs. You need that specialization. Big money can't come and buy and sell easily. So the big money in biotech is buy and hold. The small money can come in and move around. We have found a way to find partners who are small, extraordinary investors who know the signs and can figure it out. They run small amounts of money. They can put up big numbers, because they can buy and sell while the big guys can't.

headline: Collateralised specialty private credit — GP solutions, data centre construction loans, energy — earns a complexity premium; avoiding commoditised direct lending to sponsors where the edge has been competed away
reasoning: Perold describes High Vista's credit strategy as bespoke, one-loan-at-a-time collateralised lending with specialist originators in each vertical. The firm deliberately avoids direct lending to sponsors because it is commoditised, uncollateralised, and offers insufficient risk-adjusted returns. Current favourites include GP solution financing and data centre construction loans, where hyperscaler credit backstops collateral. Energy credit has become less interesting as the crowd has moved in.
quote: Our credit strategy is always based on where can I find great borrowers where making a loan in size is what they need. Fashion a loan that's highly collateralized that meets our needs takes a lot of work. For that work, we solve their problem, but we get paid an extra return. A return for the work we're putting in, it's a return for complexity. If you can do those well, that's great. We've always avoided direct lending. Lending to sponsors, uncalateralized, where you make a loan and you hope there's enough profits. That's the vast bulk of private credit is direct lending. So we've always avoided that. Because we want to see the collateral. We want to get paid for complexity. It's a far more commodity space in the lending markets.

headline: Venture capital is an essential arrow in any AI strategy — timing is impossible so sustained exposure to great VC firms is the right approach, with a barbell of established brands and newly spun-out stars

Exposure to venture and great VC firms is a fantastic way to be a disrupter. For balanced portfolio, you want both. Venture is a way of doing it. It's hard to time venture. The venture investments made in the 2010-2012, when mobile applications were beginning, a few years after the iPhone came out, incredible returns from that period. episode_title: André Perold – Investing Through Exponential Change (EP.516)

headline: Market cap down 40% in under a year despite strong earnings growth through 2028, because AI disruption has destroyed confidence in terminal value — illustrates why owning software equity requires terminal value conviction that is currently very hard to form

The earnings growth continues high and expectations offer it to continue to be spectacular through something like 2028. Beyond that, we don't know. It's croaked in price. episode_title: André Perold – Investing Through Exponential Change (EP.516)

headline: Niche corners of private credit — litigation finance, catastrophe risk, aviation finance, European distress, small-ticket mezzanine — offer bond-like returns with near-zero correlation to markets

She warns that any reduction to the super guarantee rate would leave millions of workers who relied on the system without adequate savings at retirement, replicating the pre-super era when workers retired with little savings and went straight onto the age pension. It's where you start to really get that proper uplift with a much more dignified, comfortable standard of living for millions of retirees. That is crucial. headline: Private investors now hold ~75% of Treasuries versus prior dominance by price-insensitive official buyers, making supply fluctuations more impactful at the margin than historically
reasoning: A decade ago the Fed and foreign central banks absorbed a much larger share of the Treasury market; today private investors hold roughly three-quarters of outstanding supply. Official investors like foreign central banks often buy for policy reasons and are price-insensitive, whereas private investors care about valuations and can say no. This structural shift means every additional bond now has to clear with a more discerning, price-sensitive buyer, raising the hurdle rate and making marginal supply changes more consequential than in prior cycles. However, Anshul stresses that price-sensitive buyers still weigh many factors, so supply remains one of several inputs rather than the dominant driver.
quote: I'll give you that. I think that's perhaps one of the most important developments in the market. Official investors like foreign central banks, they often buy for policy reasons. Private investors, as you can imagine, they care far more about valuations. Which means, you know, fluctuation supply should matter actually more than it used to because every additional bond, and I kind of alluded to this earlier, has to clear with an investor who can say no. Whereas in the past, some of those investors were more price-insensitive.

headline: Supply composition matters for relative value and curve trades but macro forces — growth, inflation, policy rate expectations — dominate absolute long-end yield direction
reasoning: Anshul argues that while issuance decisions do influence term premium and can matter at the margin, the dominant driver of long-term Treasury yields is the market's repricing of the expected path of short-term rates over many years. Supply only works through term premium, which is one component of the yield; expectations of growth, inflation, and policy rates are a far larger force. Most of the rise in long yields seen so far in 2025 has come from markets reassessing the path of short rates higher, not from supply dynamics. The conclusion is that debt managers can influence relative value across sectors and maturities but cannot set outright yield levels.

headline: Record $1.53T margin debt warrants vigilance but Margin/GDP ratio misread — Margin/Market Cap at 1.8-2.0% is within historical norms; rate-of-change deceleration, not static GDP threshold, is the real crash signal
reasoning: U.S. margin debt reached a record US$1.53 trillion in June 2026, up 51% year-on-year, and represents roughly 4.5% of GDP — the highest in the compiled series, above prior crash peaks. However, the author argues that GDP is the wrong denominator: margin accounts are liquidated against portfolio value, not GDP, and when margin debt is measured against total stock market capitalisation it sits at only 1.8–2.0% — well within post-2010 norms. The 'Buffett Indicator' (Market Cap/GDP) has persistently exceeded 120% since 2018 without triggering a crash, illustrating that structural shifts in the economy make century-spanning static thresholds unreliable. The real risk signal is the velocity of leverage accumulation: markets tend to peak when the rate of change of margin debt growth slows after a parabolic surge, as FOMO-driven buying exhausts incremental liquidity. By July 2026, margin debt had already fallen 5.6% from the June record to US$1.42 trillion, flagging the beginning of a potential unwind that could create cascading forced selling.
quote: Today's record US$1.53 trillion margin debt and its sharp 51 per cent surge reflect undeniable speculative fervour, and yes, it's reminiscent of the Dot-Com boom. But keep in mind the underlying collateral base supporting that debt has expanded too. Leverage is real, and the speed of its recent rise warrants some vigilance. But instead, monitor the rate of change, track market liquidity, and remember it's the sudden slowing of leverage, not an arbitrary GDP benchmark, that usually signals a turn. By July, FINRA margin debt had already fallen to US$1.42 trillion, around 5.6 per cent below the June record. The risk starts when leverage unwinds, and that unwind also causes falling prices. If that happens, then we can expect some forced selling, which can trigger more selling.

headline: China has simultaneously become the world's largest absolute emitter and the country most rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels — driven by energy security and economic competitiveness rather than climate goals — and has come to dominate solar, battery, critical minerals and EV supply chains

China's industrialisation drove 230% emissions growth but also, through necessity, prompted massive investment in renewables, motivated by the absence of domestic fossil fuel resources other than coal and the desire for energy self-sufficiency. China now dominates the solar, battery, critical minerals and EV supply chains, and its share of renewable electricity generation has shifted more aggressively than other major economies.

And China is the country that's most rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels. And with that, I mean, necessity prompts innovation. So because you had this industrialization, this rise in wealth and this emissions, you also had a lot of negative consequences of that. There was a lot of pollution. And then you saw investments by China in building out the supply chain to support more renewable energy... They have owned the solar supply chain, the battery supply chain, the critical minerals supply chain, and the EV supply chain.

headline: AI is pulling renewable investment forward and driving solar and battery storage costs down, but on a net basis AI is emissions-additive through 2030, requiring an all-of-the-above energy approach including slower coal retirements and more gas
reasoning: Cromwell argues that AI's insatiable power demand is simultaneously pulling investment in renewables forward — particularly solar and storage — because that drives down costs and broadens economic viability. However, when modelling the net effect through 2030, Wellington's best estimate is that AI is emissions-additive: meeting demand requires slower coal retirements, new gas investment, behind-the-meter gas generation, nuclear (no near-term contribution), plus large-scale solar, wind and storage. Post-2030, capital flowing into nuclear and geothermal could accelerate the transition.
quote: When you do the math, our best estimate is in order to meet the rising power demands of AI, we are going to have to have an all of the above energy approach, which means slower coal retirements. It means investment in gas. It means investment in what is called behind the meter power, which is typically gas powered. It also means investments in nuclear, but they don't really contribute over that time scale. Investments in solar, investments in wind and investments in storage. A lot of investments in those latter technologies. And when you look at it that way through 2030, we do think that AI is emissions additive.
episode_title: Necessity prompts innovation: AI and the energy transition with Wendy Cromwell

headline: National security and economic competitiveness is the most consistent theme across regions — driving a shift from global optimisation to resilience and self-reliance that is broadly inflationary but creates investment opportunities, including but not limited to defense
reasoning: Cromwell identifies national security and economic competitiveness as the dominant cross-regional investment theme, with countries seeking to build internal resilience rather than rely on a globally optimised system. quote: The most consistent theme I see across regions is this desire for national security and economic competitiveness. And when I say national security, you think, oh, defense. And that is an element of that. We have seen an uptick of interest and changing of guidelines around defense. But a broader definition of national security, this idea of self-reliance, and this idea that we're now moved into this age of resilience, where each country, each region, wants to build resilience within their own system rather than operating in a globally optimized system. And that has massive economic consequences. It's probably largely inflationary. But it also has benefits of being more immune to shocks. And it has investment ideas baked within it as well.
episode_title: Necessity prompts innovation: AI and the energy transition with Wendy Cromwell

When we looked back on that and said look we almost killed the company. What would we do differently? We said automate last. You've got to perfect the process before you automate. So at the point of transaction, that's a brilliant part of smart contracts in blockchain tech because without that, you know, you can put it into a a contract, you can say the covenant says, you know, you can't use this in other, other projects. headline: Data spending arms race has hit diminishing returns; real edge now lies in judgement, organisational speed and trust, not data spend
reasoning: Michael Skinner argues that global spending on market data and analysis has set records nearly every year for over a decade, yet active fund performance outcomes are dispersed and many active funds underperform benchmarks over ten years. He draws on the 1980 Grossman-Stiglitz theorem, which holds that information earns a return only while it is scarce. As AI is set to commoditise data further, the informational edge from data spending is eroding. Skinner concludes the real competitive advantage has shifted to judgement, organisational speed and trust rather than data expenditure.
quote: In the data arms race of investing, judgement has never been so important. In 1980, Sanford Grossman and Joseph Stiglitz published a paper with an inconvenient conclusion for anyone selling market data: information earns a return only while it is scarce. If share prices reflected all possible information and the efficient market hypothesis was true, nobody would be paid to do research, and alpha generation would be improbable, if not impossible. The market needs inefficiency to fund the people who make it efficient. Almost half a century later, the funds management industry is determined to test the theorem again. Global spending on market data and analysis has set a record nearly every year for more than a decade. Over roughly the same period, the performance scorecard is somewhat underwhelming: return outcomes are dispersed, and many active funds underperform their benchmark over ten years.
episode_title: Data and AI: Is the Data Arms Race Over?

headline: Passive investing amplifies momentum, allowing stocks to stay overpriced 6-12 months after index inclusion; best active opportunities are where forced buying exhausts itself or ahead of index adds in $300-500M cap names
reasoning: James Sioud explains that passive investing mechanically magnifies momentum: once a stock is added to indices, market participants are forced to buy it regardless of fundamentals, which can keep it expensive for 6 to 12 months. Unlike a decade ago, shorting an overpriced stock immediately at the point of inclusion is more dangerous because the momentum can run much longer. Instead, the best short ideas are where that forced-buying cycle has ended and the stock begins falling. On the long side, identifying companies in the $300-500 million market cap range where a fundamental thesis coincides with an upcoming index addition allows early entry before forced flows inflate the price.
quote: I think you just have to be honest with how passive investing works and it it's essentially a magnification of momentum. If a stock is going up, it tends to continue going up, especially when it gets added to indices. So a stock can easily get overpriced on fundamentals and stay that way for 612 months as it gets added. So various indices and as many market participants are forced to buy that company. Now maybe 10 years ago, you would short that company as it gets 10% or 30% too expensive. I think these days you have to be aware that this can run a lot longer and you have to be open to riding a momentum, but also being conscious that it will break eventually. So some of the best ideas we have are where that force buy in has run out and that stock's going to start falling. But also on the flip side, identifying companies around that 300 to $500 million market cap range where we form a fundamental view that can coincide side with an index add and allow us to get earlier in that journey before it gets too expensive and ultimately take advantage of that those forced flows in the market.

quote: Amcor offers a combination we find attractive: a globally diversified and relatively defensive business, a dividend yield above 5%, a low earnings multiple (11x), and substantial opportunities for management to improve earnings without relying on stronger economic conditions. Berry has created significant self-help. Synergies are running ahead of plan. Flexibles remains a high-margin and resilient core business. Rigids has considerable scope to close its margin gap. Non-core assets are being removed, and cash released from working capital should allow leverage to fall. Against that base case sits the optionality from volume growth. For much of the past two years, packaging volumes have been declining. FY26 ended with the first modest positive movement in some time. We do not regard one quarter as proof of a sustained recovery, but we do regard it as evidence that the negative volume drag may be easing. That matters because the earnings improvements described above have largely been achieved without much help from demand. If volumes simply stabilise, synergies, procurement and margin improvement can continue to drive earnings. If volumes return to sustained growth, Amcor should have materially greater operating leverage through the enlarged Berry platform. That is the attraction: We are not paying a high price for volume recovery, nor do we require one for the investment to work. episode_title: Bond talk: Which way interest rates?

headline: 30-year Treasury yield above 5.3% reflects genuine inflation reality and risk premium, not a crisis signal
reasoning: Queen contextualises the 30-year yield above 5.3% — its highest since 2007 — as consistent with a 2.5-3% inflation environment rather than a harbinger of crisis. episode_title: Bond talk: Which way interest rates?

headline: US debt above $40 trillion is a long-run concern but not an imminent crisis; buyer strike unlikely given reserve currency status and market liquidity
reasoning: Queen has been asked about US debt risk since 1991 and has consistently concluded it is not an immediate crisis. It has been the number one question I've been asked since 1991... the idea that the U.S. won't actually pay back its debt in currency that it prints is kind of silly. And so the real worry is you have a debt crisis because there's just a buyer strike... At the same time it is the largest most liquid rate complex in the world. It's the best economy probably in the world or best large economy in the world. So there's a lot of things working for us that probably prevents that for now.
episode_title: Bond talk: Which way interest rates?

headline: Fed's move away from forward guidance under Warsh is positive; dots and guidance exposed that central bank models are no better than the market's
reasoning: Queen argues that forward guidance, which started during the GFC to provide stimulus beyond zero rates, ended up undermining the Fed's mystique by revealing that its forecasts were no more accurate than the market's. He welcomes Kevin Warsh's intention to reduce or eliminate forward guidance, believing it restores a healthier dynamic where the market prices bonds based on economic fundamentals and the Fed's stated mandates rather than on unreliable central bank forecasts.
quote: I think it's a good idea. Personally I think that the thing that Ford guidance and the Fed dots and all of that really did was remind us that they don't know any more than anybody else does. There was this sort of illusion this this pay no attention to the man behind the curtain sense... Once forward guidance came out it was pretty clear that their models weren't any better than anybody else's. What we need to know is why are they doing what they do. What are their mandates. How are they going to go about trying to meet those.
episode_title: Bond talk: Which way interest rates?

headline: Real interest rates have normalised to a 2-3% range, making 4-5%+ nominal yields the new normal rather than an anomaly
reasoning: John Queen argues that the post-GFC era of near-zero real rates was an aberration driven by globalisation, excess global labour supply, and the need to repair the financial system. Post-COVID de-globalisation, tariff wars and re-nationalisation have reversed those deflationary forces. He calculates that pre-GFC 10-year real rates (nominal minus CPI) historically ran at 2-3%, which is where they are today, implying nominal rates of 4-5%+ are appropriate and the economy can operate well at these levels.
quote: I just went today and did a little bit of a study on real interest rates, the regular interest rate minus inflation. And if you look back pre the GFC or today, you'll see that 10-year real rates using nominal regular CPI and the regular 10-year tends to stay between about two and three percent or about where we are today. We're past this time that most people in markets are familiar with where real interest rates were between zero and one for most of the last 15 years. All of a sudden now we're back to what I think is a more normal real interest rate range. It feels uncomfortable because that means nominal interest rates are four and five plus percent. But the economy can operate quite well at that as long as it knows that's the right range.
episode_title: Bond talk: Which way interest rates?

headline: Buying Alphabet, Meta, Nvidia, Amazon bonds at high-yield-like spreads despite investment-grade quality and extraordinary cash generation
reasoning: Queen specifically calls out Google/Alphabet, Meta, Nvidia and Amazon as hyperscaler bond issuers that are trading at wide, almost high-yield-like spreads due to massive debt issuance and uncertainty about future borrowing. episode_title: Bond talk: Which way interest rates?

episode_title: Bond talk: Which way interest rates?

And then now we've got a whole problem the private credit market because the collapse of Bafla Group which is western sydney is one of their biggest developers. headline: RBA increasingly hawkish with two more rate hikes now fully priced; Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter and Andrew Hauser both signalled hawkishness this week; Australia has second-highest trimmed-mean inflation among advanced economies

Van Onselen does not expect inflation to become unsticky without a fundamental improvement in productivity.

And I think that's you know, that might be one of the reasons why the financial markets now are tipping, you know, two rate hikes are fully priced now pretty much two more... australia's inflation's just very sticky. Unfortunately, we've got the second highest trim mean inflation rate which I don't say it's in the advanced world... We were just behind norway. So I think norway was top and we were second highest.

headline: CPI rents set to rise further as advertised new rental growth of 5.7% feeds through with a lag, but affordability ceiling and household formation responses will cap the upside

However, Van Onselen argues that renters will increasingly double up, stay at home longer or move into group housing as a ceiling response. Unlike the purchase market, rents cannot be leveraged, making it a purer supply-demand play with a natural affordability limit. National vacancy rates have risen to 1.9% from 1.5%, the highest in about 18 months.
quote: I think we are also hitting a bit of affordability ceiling with rents. So it does get to a point where when rents get to such a level as a proportion of income people will stay at home for longer. You just get more group housing... it doesn't necessarily mean that rents will necessarily rise because of a you know mismatch between supply and demand like just in a basic sense because households can always group together. And I think we are seeing a bit of that now and we're likely to see more of that and that should put a bit of a ceiling on how much rents can increase because unlike the purchase market, you can't leverage rents.
episode_title: Ep. 430: The Worst Drop Is Yet to Come for House Prices (Feat. Leith Van Onselen)

headline: Biggest Australian house price correction in living memory underway, with national five-city index down 5.1% and on track to surpass the record 8.6% peak-to-trough decline by end of year

Multiple negative forces are converging simultaneously: three RBA rate hikes already delivered, with markets fully pricing two more; abolition of negative gearing for established housing and changes to the capital gains tax discount hammering investor demand; new anti-money laundering rules for residential property from July 1 ending Australia's status as a soft spot for illicit funds; slowing immigration; and fiscal austerity at state and federal level reversing pandemic-era stimulus. Van Onselen believes Australia could track similar to New Zealand and Canada, where prices have fallen high-teens nominally and around 30% in real terms over a multi-year period. The correction started from historically peak valuations, meaning mean reversion has further to run.

You know, but that could take a five-year period to get there, but I wouldn't be surprised at all if we get there because I think the this 30 year super cycle in house prices is well and truly over we've got structurally higher interest rates now and then they're not going to go back to where they were and we also started this correction from an evaluation level where basically the housing market has never been more expensive.
episode_title: Ep. 430: The Worst Drop Is Yet to Come for House Prices (Feat. Leith Van Onselen)

headline: Melbourne most likely to lead the eventual rebound: most affordable major capital, missed the post-COVID boom, and a probable change of state government in November could reverse punitive land tax settings

headline: Short since March 2026: CEO spent over nine of fifteen minutes on an unvalidated AI transformation program with no financial metrics disclosed, while twelve sell-side analysts asked zero AI questions — a textbook talk-to-substance gap in a year defined by tariff pressure and margin compression
reasoning: Plato has held a short position in Breville since March 2026. Despite record revenue of $1.81 billion (+6.7%), profit barely moved and gross margin fell 60 bps due to US tariffs and the cost of shifting manufacturing out of China; the company declined to give FY27 guidance and shares fell on the day. The CEO devoted more than nine minutes of a 15.5-minute address to an 'AI transformation program,' framing AI tokens as a new factor of production alongside labour and capital, yet disclosed no dollar spend, no technology partner, no headcount and no externally verifiable financial metric. The only numbers offered were self-generated operational metrics: over 50% of employees classified as 'amplified' with no disclosed methodology, and a '6.3x improvement' in a recipe application measured against an internal estimate of prior process time. Critically, twelve analysts from UBS, Macquarie, Goldman Sachs, Barrenjoey, RBC, Jarden and others asked zero questions about the AI program, illustrating the presentation-vs-Q&A asymmetry that Plato's screen is designed to detect. Plato flags this as one of the clearest examples of AI overstatement found in the reporting season, though notes it is not alleging impropriety or making a share-price prediction.
quote: For 2026 forward, we now have an incremental lever, AI tokens. We can now drive the flywheel with head count, tokens, and money. ... Not one dollar of spend was disclosed. No headcount, no named technology partner, and nothing on what the program had earned. The company said only that 'our total spend on the program is deliberate and controlled.' ... Twelve of them were on the call, from UBS, Macquarie, Goldman Sachs, Barrenjoey, RBC, Jarden and six other firms. Between them they did not mention AI once. Not the transformation program, not the applications, not the tokens, nothing. That is the gap our screen is built to find.
episode_title: Plato research: One in three ASX companies make unvalidated AI mentions

headline: Around 1 in 3 ASX companies (31.7%) now make unvalidated AI mentions in earnings calls — up from 1 in 7 in 2022 — flagging a systematic pattern of AI overstatement worth monitoring
reasoning: Plato's NLP models process ASX earnings calls, separating management from analyst commentary and extracting performance metrics, then flag AI references that cannot be validated against hard metrics or analyst engagement. A mention is 'unvalidated' when a company raises AI but neither reports an AI-linked metric (e.g. AI spend, copilot seats, GPU utilisation, % bookings with AI) nor draws a single analyst question. The share of ASX companies making unvalidated AI mentions has risen from roughly 14% in 2022 to 31.7% today. Three composite measures are used to rank AI overstatement: talk-to-substance ratio, presentation-vs-Q&A asymmetry, and the pattern of ramping AI narrative while quietly dropping previously disclosed metrics. The framework does not detect fraud but is designed to be an early-warning signal, as illustrated by the Presto Automation case where the screen flagged concerns before the company was delisted from Nasdaq.
quote: Today around 1 in 3 ASX companies (31.7%) make unvalidated mentions of AI, up from 1 in 7 in 2022. This is not proof of 'AI washing', since a company might raise AI in passing or when discussing external trends, but it tells us where to look.
episode_title: Plato research: One in three ASX companies make unvalidated AI mentions

headline: Case study in unvalidated AI claims: SEC found it misled investors on autonomous ordering; ~70% of orders still handled by humans; ultimately delisted from Nasdaq and forced into asset sale
reasoning: Presto Automation was a US-listed restaurant technology company that marketed AI for drive-thru ordering. On its November 2023 earnings call, the chairman repeatedly claimed Presto was 'one of the most immediately actionable and scalable vertical applications of AI today,' while admitting it was 'not yet in the numbers.' Plato's talk-to-substance ratio flagged this: many AI references with no attached figures an investor could verify. The SEC subsequently found Presto had misled investors by claiming its technology would eliminate human order-taking, when in practice humans still handled approximately 70% of orders. Presto was delisted from Nasdaq in August 2024 and its lenders forced a sale of the business in December 2024. The case is cited as evidence that the unvalidated-AI-mention screen can provide early warning ahead of material negative outcomes.
quote: Presto Automation was a US-listed restaurant technology company selling AI for drive-thru ordering. On its November 2023 earnings call, management returned to AI repeatedly, almost always without a figure attached. Its chairman told investors: 'I've said it before and I'll say it again, I believe Presto is one of the most immediately actionable and scalable vertical applications of AI today, even though I know it will take some time to reflect in the numbers.' A grand claim, with the admission that it was not yet in the numbers. That is exactly what our first measure flags: plenty of talk, nothing an investor could check. The SEC later found Presto had mislead investors, telling the market its technology would eliminate human order taking, when in practice humans were still handling around 70% of orders.
episode_title: Plato research: One in three ASX companies make unvalidated AI mentions

headline: A really good business can produce disappointing returns if priced for perfection; a mediocre company can generate excellent returns if expectations were excessively pessimistic
reasoning: Investing is not a simple mathematical formula where good fundamentals mechanically produce good returns. What matters is how a company's earnings and fundamentals compare to the collective expectations already embedded in the share price. A high-quality company whose strong performance is already anticipated will see a stagnant or disappointing share price — as illustrated by employees who receive company shares and cannot understand why strong earnings produce no price gain. Conversely, a mediocre business can outperform if market expectations were excessively negative. This is the game-theory dimension of investing: outcomes depend not just on fundamentals but on the decisions and perceptions of all other market participants.
quote: And we're not saying that company earnings and other fundamentals don't matter. They of course do. But, it also matters how they compare to everyone else's expectations. And that really matters in terms of the outcome that you will achieve. So, really good business can produce disappointing investment returns if it's priced for perfection. On the other hand, a mediocre company can generate excellent returns if those expectations were excessively pessimistic.
episode_title: Why Smart Investors Still Lose Money

headline: Extreme pessimism in April 2025 tariff turmoil drove herd selling via loss aversion, while extreme optimism fuels bubble-buying — both are prisoner's-dilemma dynamics that destroy investor returns
reasoning: During the April 2025 tariff turmoil, investor sentiment surveys and the put/call ratio showed extreme pessimism, leading investors to sell en masse to avoid being 'left holding the bag.' This is driven by loss aversion — losses feel twice as painful as equivalent gains — causing selling that begets more selling. The mirror dynamic occurs in bubbles, where investors buy not because prices are justified but because they expect someone else to pay even more tomorrow. The key insight is that this behaviour doesn't require irrationality; it simply requires investors responding to their perception of the incentives they face. The optimal path — analogous to both prisoners staying silent — is for investors to remain patient during corrections, focus on fundamentals, and avoid portfolio decisions based on anticipating what everyone else will do.
quote: And what we see in the graph is extreme pessimism that often leads to large dips in the index where investors clamor to remove themselves before others do. They don't want to be the ones that are left holding the bag. And this is an example of the concept of loss aversion where a loss feels twice as painful as an equivalent gain. And then on the other side of that, of course, is when there's extreme optimism and that is when investors are trying to get into the market to capitalize on gains that they foresee before others do that. Now, imagine a world where more investors remain patient during a market correction. Share prices would likely recover much quicker and everyone would benefit. But instead, what we actually see in real life is that many investors sell because they fear others are going to sell and they're trying to get out of the market first.
episode_title: Why Smart Investors Still Lose Money

The ATO allows six months to restructure a fund following a member's death. He emphasises that binding death benefit nominations are essential because superannuation is not automatically an estate asset dealt with via a will. His key advice is to simplify the SMSF and put succession structures in place while all members still have full capacity.

They know when the tax is due, they know when the audit's happening, they're paying the all the bills out of the fund. And then maybe one or two or three of the other members don't really take an active role. But it's very important that everybody understands a few things about their funds. First of all, who is the trustee? Do you have an individual trustee structure or corporate trustee structure? Because that makes a difference at the end of the day if you have to. If you have a member pass away or become incapable of running the fund, looking at who has power of attorney over the members of the fund as well. And, and remembering that holding an enduring power between it doesn't automatically make somebody else the trustee if they take over from you. But then we need to have that process in place. It's important for everyone to know who's getting the benefit, the binding death dominations, how that all works when someone was to pass away and what's going to happen to the assets within the fund.

And what we're seeing is really inflation moving through supply chains at different stages. So very basic commodities get interrupted first fuel and fertilizer and those sorts of things. And then we move through to more complex goods. So petrochemicals, plastics, PVC pipes, all those sorts of things all the way up to to much more complex, transformed, finished goods that takes longer for the inflation to show up in those items. headline: High-quality global rollout story; long store runway, structural gross margin gains and highly cash-generative model, but ANZ softness and capital intensity of expansion are key risks to watch
reasoning: Lovisa operates 1,136 stores across 50+ markets with an 80%+ gross margin, high ROCE, short payback periods and strong cash generation (operating cash flow $294.5m converting at 98% of EBITDA in FY26). The investment case rests on the global store rollout: 160 new openings in FY26, with Europe and the Americas each growing sales close to 30%, UK and Germany delivering 54 openings, and US landlord fit-out contributions rising 70%. Gross margin has expanded for 6 consecutive years (270bps since FY23) driven by sourcing, promotional efficiency and shrinkage control. FY26 showed EBITDA up 20.9% to $301.1m and NPAT up 10.7% to $95.6m, though ANZ comps declined 5.7% and lease costs grew ahead of sales. First 8 weeks of FY27 showed sales +16.4% and comps +3.0% with momentum improving through August, supporting the long-term thesis.
quote: Lovisa Holdings Ltd LOV) is an Australian-founded global specialty retailer of fast fashion jewellery and accessories, operating 1,136 stores across more than 50 markets. The business model is one of the more attractive in global retail: small-format corporate-owned stores of 80sqm, low fitout costs, vertically designed product sold at gross margins over 80%, and a supply chain that moves product from design to store in weeks. This combination produces high returns on capital, short payback periods on new stores and strong cash generation, with operating cash flow of $294.5m in FY26 converting at 98% of EBITDA. The investment case rests on the global store rollout. Lovisa opened 160 new stores in FY26, taking network growth to 105 net, with Europe and the Americas each growing sales close to 30%. These regions remain significantly underpenetrated relative to the mature ANZ market, and the UK and Germany delivered 54 openings between them, providing the base for continued expansion. Landlord fit-out contributions rose 70% as US landlords increasingly court the brand, a useful signal of its standing in the world's largest retail market. Gross margin has now expanded 6 consecutive years, 270bps since FY23, driven by sourcing, promotional efficiency and shrinkage, not price alone. The FY26 result showed both the strength and the tensions in the model. Sales grew 17.6% with comps 2.0%, EBITDA rose 20.9% to $301.1 m and NPAT 10.7% to $95.6m, with dividends of 86cps representing a 100% payout. Against that, the home ANZ market declined 5.7%, lease costs grew ahead of sales, and incremental margins ran below the group average as the rollout shifts toward newer, less mature markets. These are the natural economics of a global expansion phase, but they are the metrics we watch most closely, as the durability of new store returns ultimately governs how much of the long runway converts into shareholder value. Trading in the first 8 weeks of FY27 showed sales 16.4% and comps 3.0%, with momentum improving through August. With a long store runway, structural gross margin gains and a highly cash generative model funding both growth and dividends, Lovisa remains a high quality global rollout story.

headline: Australian AI data centre economics challenged: power and non-compute infrastructure capture only ~20 cents in the dollar of AI revenues, making sustainable economic rent difficult
reasoning: The fund argues that Australia's ability to capture economic rent from AI data centres is structurally limited. Power and non-compute infrastructure account for roughly 20 cents in every dollar of AI revenues, and within that, power generation captures only about 10 cents. For power generators to earn rent they need either abundant low-cost power (which Australia lacks) or the ability to negotiate elevated long-term prices. Neither is easily achievable in the current policy environment.
quote: Simplistically, sustainable economic rent on data centres in Australia should AI participation be restricted to energy supply and the infrastructure assets housing the compute assets, in which chip and memory suppliers earn the excess returns, looks like a struggle. Power and non-compute infrastructure command around 20 cents in the dollar of AI revenues. On the 10 cents or so in the dollar which flows to power generation, economic rent will rely simply on having abundant low-cost power, which Australia doesn't have, or convincing buyers to pay elevated prices over long periods.

headline: Bond yields are one of the greatest challenges to current equity valuations; equity investors ignore bond market counterparts at their peril
reasoning: The fund argues that policymakers' words assure investors of commitment to controlling inflation while their actions promote the opposite. Bond investors are seeking compensation for ballooning government debt and uncontrolled deficits, with interest payments contributing around half of the US deficit. If monetary growth slows and inflation follows, the equation skews back in favour of bond investors and removes inflation protection fuel supporting earnings and equity markets. The potential threat to asset values from the size of the global balance sheet relative to the income statement is described as significant.
quote: As the purported risk-free benchmark on which most valuation methodologies rest, bond yields are, in our view, one of the greatest challenges to current equity valuations. Corporate profits, the financial economy and the asset values we count as wealth cannot be sustained and grow if the debt on the other side of the global balance sheet collapses or stops growing. As bond investors seek compensation for the risk of ballooning government debt and uncontrolled deficits - partly driven by escalating interest payments, which already contribute around half of the US deficit - the positioning of equity investors in gold and commodities is a wager they will be entirely unsuccessful. headline: Global crude flow reshuffle underway as Venezuela barrels shift from China to US Gulf Coast and India, creating a quality-of-crude mismatch
reasoning: Sahdev explains that Venezuelan heavy crude historically required light naphtha inputs from Russia, China, and Iran, with output flowing to China. However, US Gulf refineries have a limit on heavy barrel intake, so India — with complex refineries like Reliance and Indian Oil capable of processing heavy, sour Venezuelan crude — becomes a beneficiary. China has effectively lost Venezuelan, Iranian, and some Russian barrels simultaneously, creating a multilayered reshuffle of crude, naphtha, and fuel oil flows he calls 'chem politics.'
quote: India in that case is a bit of a lucky advantage because India has very complex refineries like Reliance and Indian Oil, which can process the dirty, heavy, sort of toxic, I would say Venezuelan kind of crudes at an advantage price. headline: Premiums and discounts to NTA in LICs are driven by supply/demand dynamics, not just portfolio performance — dividends, shareholder communication, and buyback efficacy all play key roles
reasoning: Jesse Hamilton explains that LIC premiums and discounts are fundamentally a supply-and-demand phenomenon. Strong performance alone does not guarantee a premium, and poor performance does not guarantee a discount — shareholder communication and understanding of the investment strategy matter equally. Above-market fully franked dividend yields can attract demand and push a stock to a premium, while insufficient yield can cause persistent discounts. On-market buybacks are mathematically accretive to remaining shareholders' NTA per share but in practice do not durably close discounts because they absorb supply temporarily without creating new demand; once stopped, the supply returns. A company conducting a buyback also signals to Hamilton that management sees no better use of capital than buying back shares rather than investing in the market.
quote: People would think that they are, but in practice for listed investment companies, they don't have much of an impact. And it sounds a little bit counterintuitive. Mathematically buybacks work. You're buying back shares in the company at less than what they're worth. So the arithmetic stacks up where it actually increases the value of the NTA per share for the remaining shareholders. And I can understand why companies do it. But when you get back to why companies trade at a premium or discount, a buyback doesn't change the supply and demand dynamic. It soaks up supply, but it doesn't stop it and it doesn't create new demand. So what you tend to find is when companies might be conducting an onmarket buyback, it works for a short period of time and the minute you stop that buyback, the supply is still there and there's no new demand. So whilst buybacks sort of work in theory from a mathematics standpoint, in practice they don't work. And when I look at a company doing a buyback, the first thing that signals to me is there's no better use for the capital.
episode_title: Understanding Premiums and Discounts in Listed Investment Companies

headline: Flags that a divided government post-midterms raises debt ceiling and government shutdown risks, with distinct market implications for each
reasoning: A divided government outcome from the 2026 midterms would likely increase fiscal noise around recurring deadlines including government funding and the debt ceiling. Salvatore differentiates the market impact of each: shutdowns primarily have indirect effects by degrading or delaying government economic data, hampering decision-making by investors and the Fed. By contrast, the debt ceiling has a more direct market impact, showing up in the Treasury bill market where bills maturing near a potential X-date cheapen relative to other short-term benchmarks as investors price in default risk, even when resolution remains the base case.
quote: If we get a divided government in November, that typically means more fiscal noise around the recurring deadlines, like government funding and the debt ceiling. Those two matter for markets in very different ways. A shutdown's bigger effect tends to be indirect. So think delayed or lower-quality government data, since agencies can end up working from smaller survey samples. That leaves investors and the Fed making decisions with less complete information for weeks at a stretch sometimes. The debt ceiling is more direct. That shows up most clearly in the Treasury bill market. Bills maturing around a potential deadline tend to cheapen relative to other short-term benchmarks, as investors have to price default risk into that narrow window. And that's the case even when a resolution is still the base case.
episode_title: The Politics Behind the Rising U.S. Debt

reasoning: Post the 2024 US election, tariff rhetoric drove large metal flows into the US, including platinum, gold, silver and copper, as end-users pre-positioned ahead of potential tariffs. On NYMEX/CME, a steepening of the futures forward curve created arbitrage opportunities that required physical collateral, further pulling platinum into bonded US warehouses. Chinese imports of platinum have significantly exceeded trackable end demand, suggesting government or corporate stockpiling. These flows reduce global liquidity and mean that when prompt market shortages arise, price moves are outsized.
quote: We saw huge metal flows into the US. And this isn't just platinum. It happened with gold, silver, copper as well. But end users were moving platinum into the US and stockpiling it because it wasn't clear whether the platinum was going to be tariffed in the future... We've seen a lot of metal going to China. In fact, one of the things that is quite hard to explain is where that metal has been going, because we can track Chinese end demand. But their imports have been significantly higher than that.

headline: Platinum is essential for green hydrogen production and utilisation, with more than 80% of industrial end uses linked to emissions reduction and energy efficiency
reasoning: Excluding investment and jewellery, more than 80% of platinum's industrial end uses are associated with reducing harmful emissions or reducing energy requirements in industrial processes. Platinum is described as absolutely essential to the production and utilisation of green hydrogen as an energy carrier alternative to fossil fuels. This structural demand driver, combined with AI and renewable energy applications, means the demand risk profile is skewed to the upside relative to Sturke's conservative base case of flat demand.
quote: If you look at platinum's end uses, and if you exclude investments and you exclude jewelry, more than 80% of platinum's end uses are associated with reducing harmful emissions and reducing energy requirements in industrial processes. And very specifically, it's also key for the hydrogen economy. So for the production and then utilization of green hydrogen as an energy carrier, as an alternative to using fossil fuels, that platinum is absolutely essential to that process.

headline: Palladium faces long-term structural demand headwind from internal combustion engine decline, creating mining investment uncertainty for PGM producers
reasoning: Palladium and rhodium are predominantly used in catalytic converters for internal combustion engine vehicles. As the global drivetrain electrifies over the next 10-15 years, this creates high uncertainty for more than 80% of palladium's demand profile. This makes it very difficult for mining companies to justify expanding deep-level underground PGM mines, since the economics depend on the full basket of metals including palladium and rhodium, not just platinum. The result is a structural constraint on future platinum supply even as its own demand outlook is positive.
quote: The problem is that two of the other metals, palladium and rhodium, are mostly used in catalytic converters for passenger vehicles with internal combustion engines. And, you know, in that sort of time frame in the future, we think that internal combustion engines, hybrid vehicles and so on, vehicles that need catalyzed exhaust treatment systems, we think that the tail is going to be fairly long. But nonetheless, when you've got more than 80 percent of your demand profile dependent upon, you know, internal combustion engine vehicles, sort of 10 to 15 years in the future, that creates quite a high degree of uncertainty. So making the investment decision and expanding or building new mines right now, I think is really difficult.

headline: World Platinum Investment Council director argues platinum has most attractive underlying fundamentals of any precious metal, with supply deficits set to persist into the 2030s
reasoning: Platinum has been in sustained supply deficit for three years, with above-ground stocks drawn down to the point of shortage. Mine supply is highly inelastic — deep-level underground operations require an 8-year development timeline and are difficult to flex. Demand is expected to be supported by AI data centre buildout, the hydrogen economy, and energy transition applications, which together may more than offset declining automotive catalytic converter demand. Supply deficits are forecast to continue until at least the 2030s. Platinum offers a higher beta (1.3x) to gold with an upside skew, making it the most attractive precious metal on fundamentals according to Sturke.
quote: I think if I look across the whole of the press metal complex, it's probably got the most attractive underlying fundamentals. So I mean, if we think about the platinum price, and you mentioned obviously that it had been kind of plus minus $1000 an ounce for quite a long time in the past, and then began to rally in May of last year... we were three years into sustained market deficits. So effectively, platinum supply was very constrained... above-ground stocks were just depleted to the point where there was a shortage of metal in the market.

headline: Gold continues to benefit from reserve bank buying and dollar debasement trade, with central bank accumulation likely to persist
reasoning: Gold functions effectively as a non-US dollar fiat currency, with value ascribed through millennia of use as a currency and, more recently, as a reserve asset. Concerns about US dollar management have driven significant central bank gold buying over the past 12 years, and this trend is likely to continue. Gold remains the primary beneficiary of the hard-asset rotation, but its scarcity in freely available form creates spillover into other precious metals.
quote: In my opinion right now, gold is the non-US dollar. I mean gold is a fiat currency as much as anything else really... More recently, in the last 150 odd years, it's become a reserve currency. You know, so central banks hold it as a reserve asset. And I think that with the concerns around the kind of the US management of the US dollar, you've seen significant reserve bank buying of gold over the last 12 years or so. And I think for gold, that's just likely to continue.
