headline: South African PGM mine supply, representing ~70% of global platinum output, is geologically constrained and unlikely to expand materially given 8-year development timelines and multi-metal economics
reasoning: Approximately 70% of global platinum mine supply comes from the Bushveld Igneous Complex in South Africa, a single massive deposit where mines are increasingly moving deeper, raising costs and capital requirements. An additional ~11% comes from Russia. Mine economics are determined by the full PGM basket plus byproducts, not platinum alone, making investment decisions complex. Expanding or building new mines requires approximately 8 years of development. The combination of geological concentration, deep-level operational challenges, and uncertain palladium/rhodium demand makes new supply expansion unlikely, reinforcing persistent platinum deficits.
quote: About 70 percent comes from South Africa... then you've got about 11 percent that comes from Russia... these are deep level underground mines... the economics are determined not just by platinum, but by the rest of its five other platinum group metals, plus copper, gold, chrome and all these other byproducts that these mines produce. So the challenge really from a mining perspective is to develop or expand these deep level mines is is really a sort of eight year kind of time frame.

reasoning: Sandfire completed a remarkable multi-year transformation, moving from US$430mn net debt in June 2023 to US$353mn net cash by FY26, with EBITDA rising from US$246mn to US$867mn and shares from $5.90 to ~$23. quote: This combination is what continues to attract us to Sandfire. headline: Avoids the property development sector as too hard for compounding investors
reasoning: Property development by its nature requires constant recycling of capital: operators take risk to improve assets, then must sell or monetise and start again rather than compounding returns. This means investors face an ever-compounding element of risk rather than reward. The bigger the company gets the larger the bets required and the higher execution risk becomes. Stockland's 10-year results demonstrate this with every good year followed by excess risk in the next. Coleman also notes most Australians already have heavy property exposure through their own homes and investment properties, making additional listed property exposure redundant.
quote: the challenge in property development and property ownership from a compounding point of view if you want to think of investing as the goal of compounding growth year after year until hopefully an infinite time horizon though none of us will ever live that long is that in the property development game what they call a pipeline we as an investor have to call starting over because the nature of the business is to take something unloved put risk and capital into it to make it better and then having completed that exercise rather than sitting back and enjoying the fruits of your labor you have to either sell it or monetize it and then go again and so as an investor you are going to experience in the property sector in general in Stockland is no no unique beast in that a constantly compounding element of risk rather than reward because the bigger they get the bigger the gambles they have to take the higher the execution risk comes the more likelihood that you can't get one part of that pipeline right.

headline: Andrew Coleman avoids Zip and the buy now pay later sector as structurally dangerous lending to those banks won't touch
reasoning: Buy now pay later, private credit, subprime and B-grade lending all share the same fundamental flaw: they lend to people or companies that banks will not lend to, at rates those borrowers would never pay at a bank. As long as the economy is strong repayments continue, but at the first sign of weakness the customers in that socioeconomic band default disproportionately. External investors cannot properly evaluate the loan book quality and therefore face catastrophic information asymmetry: making one to two percent on each loan when it goes well and losing 100% when it goes badly.
quote: the challenge with any business model whether it's a buy now pay later whether it's a B grade lender whether it's private credit that involves you taking risk by giving people money who can't get that money from other easier avenues is that as long as the economy continues strongly you're probably okay that money will be repaid people don't tend to take on debts they have no intention of ever repaying the challenge is that as soon as there's any weakness in the economy the customers who repay the least the quickest are those of course who are in that socio-economic band if it's individuals or companies in that lower level of earnings band who couldn't borrow money from banks... by now pay later private credit B grade finance subprime lending whatever you want to call it it changes its name every few years is all about lending to people the banks won't lend to at rates that they would never have to pay at the bank and that means it's always a house of cards because the more you grow the more risk you take on that somewhere in your lending book is a big cohort of customers that if something goes wrong they won't be repaying.

headline: Gaphen argues Fed silence undermines monetary policy transmission: markets cannot efficiently transmit policy without knowing the Fed's reaction function
reasoning: Gaphen disagrees with the notion that by communicating less, the Fed gets an unbiased market signal. He argues the Fed is not a referee but an active participant — effectively the 800-pound gorilla — in financial markets, and that monetary policy must transmit through financial markets to achieve its objectives. Without knowing the Fed's framework, tools, and intended usage, markets become inefficient transmitters of monetary policy. This could reduce the overall effectiveness of monetary policy in achieving price stability and maximum employment.
quote: I don't think that there's a world where you get the unvarnished market expectation independent of the Fed. So, I don't personally agree in the analogy of the market should play the ball and not the referee. The Fed is not a referee in markets. The Fed is a player in markets. Monetary policy acts through financial markets to achieve a set of financial conditions to deliver price stability and maximum employment. So, the Fed and markets are on the field at the same time. The Fed in some ways is the 800-pound gorilla on the field at the same time. So, everybody else on the field has to know what the gorilla is doing in order to do what they're supposed to do. You could diminish the effectiveness of monetary policy if you don't tell the market at least what your framework is and what your reaction function is and the tools that you intend to use and how you would intend to use them, then the market could be an inefficient transmitter of monetary policy.

headline: Lacalle sees loss of confidence in reserve currencies as fundamentally tied to real losses on long-term sovereign debt holdings.
reasoning: Lacalle defines 'loss of confidence' in a reserve currency in precise investment terms: it occurs when holding the long-term debt of reserve-currency issuers generates losses in real terms, and sometimes in nominal terms. A reserve asset must provide stability, strength, and real returns above inflation over time; when it fails to do so, central banks globally lose confidence in both the instrument and the underlying currency. This is the mechanism through which reserve currency transitions historically occur.
quote: What makes a change is what many people understand is loss of confidence. But when we hear loss of confidence in the US dollar or in the euro or in whatever currency, very few people can pin what that loss of confidence means. And ultimately what it means is that holding the long term debt of these countries is generating losses in real terms and sometimes in nominal terms. That's why you lose confidence in that instrument and with it lose confidence in the currency.

headline: Lacalle argues governments have breached all three limits of debt credibility — economic, fiscal, and inflationary — undermining confidence in sovereign debt as a reserve asset.
reasoning: Lacalle contends that state-issued money is effectively government debt, and that the credibility of any currency rests on three limits: the economic limit (debt growing faster than GDP with stagnating productivity), the fiscal limit (deficits and interest burdens becoming unsustainable despite central bank support), and the inflationary limit (exceeded in 2020-21 when monetary excess caused a global inflation surge). He argues that all three limits have now been breached across major developed economies, eroding the foundational rationale for sovereign debt as a reserve of value. This undermines the traditional basis for reserve currency status.
quote: governments have surpassed all of the limits that give them credibility to maintain their debt as a reserve of value. And those limits are the economic limit, the fiscal limit, and the inflationary limit. The first is the economic limit, which shows that despite increasing indebtedness and i.e. stimulating the economy, the economy does not grow, productivity growth stagnates, and debt continues to rise faster than GDP. The second one is the fiscal limit... deficits continue to rise, those deficits become unsustainable, and the burden of interest expense in the budget of governments arises to levels that become incredibly dangerous. And the third one is the inflationary limit, which was clearly exceeded in 2020-2021.
episode_title: MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Currency

headline: Lacalle sees the US dollar retaining its fiat reserve currency status by default but forecasts inevitable decentralisation as crypto competition forces fiscal discipline on governments.

He believes fiat currencies and independent decentralised currencies will coexist, and that competition from crypto assets will force governments to be more prudent with fiscal and monetary policy — echoing Hayek's argument in 'Choice in Currency' about currency competition combating inflationary incentives. He does not see the dollar being immediately displaced in the fiat world but views technological decentralisation as an unstoppable long-term force that will benefit citizens by limiting government inflation.
quote: My opinion is that cryptocurrencies, that Bitcoin, that decentralized currencies and fiat currencies are going to coexist and that if the US government really reigns on its massive imbalances, the US dollar will continue to be the world fiat reserve currency because there is no alternative in the fiat world, i.e. The dollar is not the world reserve currency in the fiat world because it's better, but because the alternatives are worse... the competition between currencies is going to be beneficial for citizens because it's going to be the best way to combat the risk of inflation when we understand that inflation is created by governments to dilute their commitments in the future.

headline: Montgomery Small Companies Fund holds FDC Consolidated Holdings after strong post-listing momentum, with shares hitting all-time high of $3.89 against $3.00 IPO price.
reasoning: FDC listed on ASX at $3.00 per share in July 2026 and has since traded as high as $3.89, an all-time high at time of writing. The company reported 13 per cent revenue growth to $1.69 billion for FY2026, with underlying EBIT up 18 per cent to $96.5 million and normalised NPAT up 14 per cent to $70.8 million. The balance sheet is strong, with $362 million in cash and no debt. Work on hand of $2.5 billion supports 89 per cent of forecast FY2027 revenue, and reaffirmed guidance calls for 12 per cent revenue growth to $1.9 billion and normalised EBIT of $100 million. Around two-thirds of work is negotiated rather than tendered, and 90 per cent of top-20 clients have delivered repeat business over the past four years, underpinning high near-term forecast confidence.
quote: At 30 June 2026, work on hand was $2.5 billion, supporting 89 per cent of the forecast revenue for the year to June 2027.
